title: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
summary: Why B+trees update pages in place and LSM-trees buffer, flush and merge sorted runs; how leveled and tiered compaction trade write, read and space amplification.
outcomes: Explain why a random small update to a B+tree rewrites a whole page and estimate the write amplification
Trace an LSM write through WAL, memtable, flush and SSTables, and a read from newest to oldest
Simulate a compaction merge, including when tombstones can be dropped
Compute write, read and space amplification for leveled vs tiered compaction
Choose between a B+tree and an LSM-tree for a workload and diagnose compaction debt

lessons.title: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it

blocks.md:
Every storage engine answers the same two questions: where does a new key-value pair go on disk, and how do I find it again? The **B+tree** answers "in its sorted position, right now". The **LSM-tree** (log-structured merge-tree) answers "anywhere cheap for now, sort it out later". This course is about what each answer costs.

From the previous course you know that durability comes from appending to a **write-ahead log** (WAL) and calling `fsync`. Both engines keep a WAL. They differ in what happens to the data *after* it is logged.

A **B+tree** is a balanced search tree stored in fixed-size **pages** (PostgreSQL uses 8 kB pages by default). Inner nodes hold guide keys and child pointers; leaves hold the keys and values (or row ids), and neighbouring leaves are linked by **sibling pointers**. Every leaf is at the same depth, and lookups, inserts and deletes are $O(\log n)$.

The important word for this course is **in place**: an insert or update finds the one leaf page where the key belongs and modifies that page.

blocks.title: A tiny B+tree: lookup, insert, split, range scan

scenes.caption: Each box is one fixed-size page. Lookup(7) reads the root, follows the guide keys to the 5 to 8 child, then searches that leaf: one page per level.
Insert(10): find the leaf for 10, add the key in sorted order inside the page. The leaf now holds 3 keys, the maximum in this toy tree. One page is modified in place.
Insert(11): the leaf would need 4 keys, so it splits into two half-full leaves and the middle key 11 is copied up into the parent. One logical insert dirtied 3 pages.
Range scan 6 to 13: descend once to the first leaf, then walk the sibling pointers. Keys come out already sorted, which is why B+trees are good at ranges.

blocks.md:
How deep is a real tree? Assume 8 KiB pages and 16-byte entries (8-byte key, 8-byte pointer): $8192 / 16 = 512$ slots, so call it about **500 children per node** after headers. For 1 billion keys:

- 2,000,000 leaves, 4,000 nodes above them, 8 above those, and 1 root: **4 levels**.
- The top three levels are 4,009 pages, about 33 MB. That fits easily in RAM, so a point lookup typically costs **one disk read** (the leaf).

This is why B+trees are the default for read-heavy, order-preserving indexes.

blocks.caption: F is the fanout (children per node), N the number of keys. Simplified: real nodes are not always full.

blocks.prompt: Rows are 100 bytes, pages are 8 KiB, and updates hit random keys in a table far larger than RAM. Roughly how many bytes reach the disk per updated row, ignoring the WAL?
blocks.reveal: About **8,192 bytes**, the whole page. A random update rarely shares a page with another pending update, so each one dirties a separate page and each page is written back in full: $8192 / 100 \approx 82$x **write amplification** (bytes written to storage divided by bytes written by the user). Each of those writes also lands at a random location on the device.

blocks.title: Updating one small row rewrites a whole page

scenes.caption: An 8 KiB page, drawn as 8 cells of about 1 KiB each (roughly 10 rows of 100 bytes per cell). The cached copy matches the copy on disk.
UPDATE changes one 100-byte row. Only a tiny part of one cell differs, but the cached page is now dirty.
Write-back works in pages, so all 8192 bytes go to the device to persist 100 changed bytes: about 82x write amplification in this simplified model (the WAL record is extra).

blocks.md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

Misconception: "B+trees always have 80x write amplification." If updates cluster (sequential keys, hot pages), many changes share one page write and the amplification drops. The 82x figure is the typical case for random updates to a cold, large table; splits and full-page images in the WAL can make it worse.

The LSM-tree paper (O'Neil, Cheng, Gawlick and O'Neil, 1996) started from exactly this problem: keeping a B-tree index on a fast-growing history table would "effectively double the I/O cost of the transaction". Their fix was to defer and batch index changes so that disk writes become large and sequential. The next lesson builds that idea.

blocks.question: A leaf split in this course's toy tree turned one insert into 3 page writes. Which statement best explains why that is still acceptable for a B+tree?
options: Splits happen only when a leaf overflows, which is rare relative to inserts that fit, so the average cost stays near one page per insert
Splits are free because the new page is written sequentially at the end of the file
The parent node is never written to disk, only kept in memory
B+trees avoid splits entirely by keeping pages half empty forever
blocks.explain: A leaf with room for hundreds of entries splits once per hundreds of inserts. The amortized cost is dominated by rewriting the one leaf page, not by splits. Parents are persisted too (they are pages like any other), and the new page can land anywhere in the file.

blocks.question: A B+tree index has 4 levels and the top 3 are cached. A workload switches from point lookups to random 100-byte updates on a table 50x larger than RAM. What dominates the new cost?
options: Extra disk reads to traverse the inner nodes
CPU time spent on binary search within pages
Rewriting a full page at a random location for each small update
Rebalancing the tree after every update
blocks.explain: Inner nodes are cached, so traversal stays cheap. Each update still needs its leaf read (one random read) and eventually a full-page random write. Updates in place do not change the tree shape, so no rebalancing happens.

lessons.title: The LSM write path: memtable, flush and immutable SSTables

blocks.md:
The LSM-tree's core move: **never modify data on disk in place**. Writes go to memory first, and memory is written out in large sorted batches. The 1996 paper called the in-memory part $C_0$ and the disk part $C_1$; LevelDB and RocksDB call them the **memtable** and **SSTables** (sorted string tables).

If the machine crashes, the memtable is lost, so every write is also appended to a write-ahead log first. After a flush makes the data durable in an SSTable, that log segment is no longer needed.

blocks.title: The LSM write path and read path

scenes.caption: A Put appends the record to the WAL (your prereq: this is what makes it durable) and inserts it into the memtable, a sorted in-memory structure. No data page on disk is touched.

When the memtable reaches its size limit (RocksDB write_buffer_size, 64 MB by default) it is frozen and a fresh memtable takes new writes, so writers usually do not wait for the disk (they stall only if flushes fall behind).

A background thread writes the frozen memtable, already sorted, as one new immutable file: an SSTable (sorted string table). One large sequential write. The matching old WAL segment can now be deleted.
Flushes keep adding files whose key ranges overlap. Compaction (lessons 3 and 4) merges them into larger non-overlapping files in lower levels.
A Get checks the newest data first: memtable, then the immutable memtable, then every L0 file newest to oldest, then at most one file per lower level. The first hit wins.

blocks.md:
Two consequences fall straight out of immutability:

- **Overwrites** do not replace the old value. The new version is simply written later, into a newer memtable or file, and newer always wins on read.
- **Deletes** are writes too. A delete inserts a **tombstone** (LevelDB calls it a deletion marker) that hides older versions of the key.

So the same key can exist in several files at once. Watch it happen.

blocks.title: Five puts, a flush, an overwrite and a delete

scenes.caption: Puts arrive in the order 3, 7, 1. The memtable keeps them sorted by key regardless of arrival order. (Toy limit: 5 entries per memtable.)
Puts 9 and 5 arrive. The memtable is full and sorted: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
Flush: the memtable is written out unchanged as SST-1, a sorted, immutable file. The memtable starts empty.
New writes: put 3=b (an overwrite), delete 5, put 8 and 2. The delete cannot touch SST-1, which is immutable, so it is written as a tombstone: a marker that says "5 is deleted".
Flush again: SST-2 holds the newer entries. Key 3 and key 5 now each exist twice on disk. Old versions still take space until compaction removes them.
Get(3): memtable miss, SST-2 hit, return b. SST-1's older 3:a is never read because newer sources are checked first.
Get(5): SST-2 has a tombstone, so the answer is "not found" and the search stops, even though SST-1 still holds 5:a.
Get(7): SST-2 covers keys 2 to 8, so its min/max range cannot rule 7 out and a naive engine searches it for nothing. Then SST-1 hits. Each extra file is extra read work.

blocks.md: LSM reads search from newest to oldest and stop at the first entry for the key, whether that is a value or a tombstone. Correctness depends only on this ordering, never on old versions being gone.

blocks.prompt: Without any further mechanism, the workload keeps writing: one new SSTable per 64 MB of writes. What happens to a Get for a key that does not exist, after 1,000 flushes?
blocks.reveal: It must check **all 1,000 files**: none can prove the key is absent except by searching it. Read cost grows without bound, and so does disk space, because overwritten values and tombstoned keys are never removed. LSM-trees fix both with **compaction** (merging files) and fix most wasted lookups with per-file **Bloom filters**. Both come next.

blocks.md: Misconception: "a delete in an LSM-tree frees space immediately." It adds data: a tombstone. Space comes back only when compaction merges the tombstone with every older version of that key and can finally drop both.

blocks.question: A Get(5) checks the memtable (miss), then finds 5:del in SST-2. SST-1 contains 5:a. What does the Get return?
options: 5:a, because SST-1 holds an actual value
Not found, because the newer tombstone hides every older version
An error, because the key exists in two files
It depends on which file has the larger key range
blocks.explain: The search runs newest to oldest and stops at the first entry for the key. The tombstone in SST-2 is newer than 5:a in SST-1, so the key is deleted. Multiple versions are normal in an LSM-tree, not an error.

blocks.question: Why can an LSM-tree accept writes faster than a B+tree on the same disk for random keys?
options: Its memtable is persisted with no fsync
It stores less data per key
It turns many random small writes into a few large sequential file writes, after logging them
It skips the write-ahead log for inserts
blocks.explain: Both engines log to a WAL. The difference is what follows: a B+tree dirties a random page per update, while an LSM-tree sorts writes in memory and flushes them as one large sequential SSTable. It stores the same data, often more temporarily, because old versions linger.

lessons.title: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels

blocks.md:
A **sorted run** is a set of entries sorted by key with at most one entry per key, stored as one or more files. Every flushed SSTable is a sorted run. **Compaction** takes several sorted runs, merges them into one, and deletes the inputs. While merging it keeps only the newest version of each key, which is what reclaims space from overwrites and deletes.

Because the inputs are already sorted, the merge is a single streaming pass, the same as the merge step of merge sort. The engine reads and writes whole files sequentially.

blocks.title: Compacting SST-2 (newer) with SST-1 (older)

scenes.caption: Inputs: newer = [2:b, 3:b, 5:del, 8:b], older = [1:a, 3:a, 5:a, 7:a, 9:a]. Both are sorted, so one forward pass over each is enough, like the merge step of merge sort.
Key 1 exists only in the older run, so it is copied as is.
Key 2 is smaller than older's 3, so it comes from the newer run.
Key 3 is in both runs. The newer version wins and the older 3:a is skipped: this is how overwritten values finally disappear.
Key 5: the tombstone shadows 5:a. Because this output is the bottommost level, no older 5 can exist anywhere below, so the tombstone is dropped too. Both entries vanish.
Keys 7 and 8 interleave from the two runs.
Key 9 finishes the older run. Result: 6 live entries from 9 inputs, one sorted run with exactly one version per key.

blocks.md: A tombstone can only be dropped when no older version of the key can exist below the output. LevelDB states the rule directly: deletion markers are dropped only if no higher-numbered level has a file whose range overlaps the key. Drop it too early and the old value comes back to life.

**Leveled compaction** (LevelDB, and RocksDB's default) organizes runs into levels:

- **L0** holds flushed files, which may overlap each other. When L0 reaches `level0_file_num_compaction_trigger` files (4 by default in both LevelDB and RocksDB), they are merged into L1.
- **L1 and below** are each a single sorted run, range-partitioned into files (RocksDB `target_file_size_base` is 64 MB by default).
- Each level has a size target about 10x the previous one (`max_bytes_for_level_multiplier` = 10). When a level is over target, one of its files is merged with the overlapping files of the next level.

blocks.title: Leveled compaction picks one file and its overlaps

scenes.caption: Below L0, each level is one sorted run split into files with non-overlapping key ranges. A Get needs at most one file per level: binary search on file boundaries, then inside the file.
L1 is over its size target. Compaction picks one L1 file, here keys 40 to 59.

It also takes every L2 file whose range overlaps 40 to 59: three files, because L2's boundaries do not line up with L1's. Simplified: with a 10x size ratio LevelDB's notes give about 12 overlapping files as the worst case.
Merge the 4 inputs (as in the code above) and write new L2 files covering 38 to 67, then delete the inputs. The rest of the tree is untouched, so other compactions can run in parallel.

blocks.md: Since RocksDB 8.4 the default is `level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes` = true: the last level's target is its actual size and each level above is 10x smaller. Levels whose target would be too small stay empty, and L0 compactions skip straight to the first level with a valid target.

blocks.title: RocksDB level targets for a 276 GB database (GB)

scenes.caption: RocksDB's documented example: max_bytes_for_level_base 1 GB, multiplier 10, last level holding 276 GB. Targets are set from the last level upward, each 10x smaller; L1 and L2 fall below the minimum and stay empty.
About 90% of the data sits in the last level and 9% in the one above. Even if every upper-level byte were a stale duplicate, space amplification would be about 1.11 (simplified: L0 adds a little).

blocks.prompt: Leveled compaction keeps each level as one sorted run. A byte that arrives in L1 will later be merged into L2, which is 10x larger. How many bytes of L2 are rewritten alongside it, in the worst case?
blocks.reveal: About **10**. To insert a slice of L1 into L2, the compaction must rewrite the overlapping slice of L2, which holds about 10x as much data for the same key range. That repeats at every level, so leveled compaction's write amplification is roughly (size ratio) x (number of levels). Lesson 4 counts it exactly.

blocks.md: Compaction converts a growing pile of overlapping files into a few large sorted runs. It is what keeps LSM reads and space bounded, and it is paid for with extra writes: every byte is rewritten each time it moves down a level.

blocks.question: A compaction merges L1 into L2 and finds a tombstone for key 42. L3 has a file covering keys 30 to 60. What must the compaction do with the tombstone?
options: Drop it, since the newer data has already been merged
Keep it in the output, because an older version of 42 may still exist in L3
Delete the L3 file covering key 42
Convert it into a regular value with an empty string
blocks.explain: L3 is older data. If the tombstone were dropped, a later Get(42) would miss in L1 and L2, reach L3 and return the old, deleted value. The marker must travel down until no lower level can hold the key.

blocks.question: Why does L0 behave differently from L1 and below in leveled compaction?
options: L0 files are compressed and others are not
L0 lives in memory
L0 files are direct memtable flushes, so their key ranges overlap and a read must check each one
L0 is always larger than L1
blocks.explain: Each flush writes whatever keys the memtable held, typically spanning the whole key space. So L0 files overlap, a Get checks every L0 file, and an L0 to L1 compaction usually takes all L0 files. Below L0, files in a level never overlap.

lessons.title: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost

blocks.md:
Three ratios describe every storage engine (definitions from the RocksDB tuning guide):

- **Write amplification**: bytes written to storage / bytes written by the user.
- **Read amplification**: disk reads per query.
- **Space amplification**: bytes on disk / bytes of live data.

RocksDB's guide works an example with leveled compaction: L1 = 512 MB, multiplier 10, 500 GB of data, so levels of 0.5 GB, 5 GB, 51 GB, 512 GB. Every byte is written to L0 (1), compacted into L1 with about equal-sized data (2), then into each of three lower levels alongside 10x more data (10 each).

blocks.caption: Write and space amplification for the RocksDB tuning guide's 500 GB leveled example. The RocksDB compaction wiki calls the per-level 10 a worst case; real compactions often do better.

blocks.md: **Tiered compaction** (Cassandra calls it size-tiered; RocksDB calls its version **universal**) makes the opposite trade. Instead of merging a small run into a big one immediately, it waits until several runs of similar size exist and merges them together. A byte is rewritten about once per level instead of about T times, but more runs sit side by side, and reads must check them all.

scenes.caption: Every flush adds a run of size 1 at the front. With a trigger of 5 runs, the 5th flush starts a compaction. Simplified as in the RocksDB wiki: only the size-ratio rule, size_ratio = 0.
Starting from the newest, add the next run while it is no larger than the total so far: 1/1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 all qualify. Result: one run of 5. Bytes written so far: 5 flushed + 5 compacted = 10.

Four more flushes give 1 1 1 1 5. The four 1s merge, but 5 > 4 so the old run is left alone: 4 5. Total written after 9 flushes: 18. Merging similar-sized runs means old data is not rewritten every time.
The pattern continues: 1 1 1 4 5 becomes 3 4 5 (flush 12), then 1 1 3 4 5 becomes 2 3 4 5 (flush 14). Runs accumulate, so a read may have to check 5 or 6 of them.
Flush 16 gives 1 1 2 3 4 5, and every run qualifies (2/2, 3/4, 4/7, 5/11), so all 6 merge into one run of 16. While it runs, inputs and output coexist: about 2x the space, briefly.
After the major compaction: one run of 16. Total bytes written for 16 units of user data: 46, a write amplification of 2.875 on this tiny tree. It grows slowly (about 1 per level) as data grows.

blocks.md: A simple model makes the trade explicit. Let $T$ be the size ratio between levels and $R$ the data size divided by the memtable size. Then there are about $L = \log_T R$ levels:

blocks.caption: Upper-bound model following the RocksDB wiki taxonomy: leveled rewrites up to T bytes per level, tiered about 1, and tiered keeps several runs per level.

blocks.title: Size ratio T: write cost vs runs to check (model)

y.label: bytes rewritten per byte, or runs

scenes.caption: R = 7812 is 500 GB of data over 64 MB memtables, giving 3.9 levels at T = 10. Leveled pays up to about T per level: 38.9. Tiered pays about 1 per level: 3.9. Simplified upper-bound model.
Leveled keeps one run per level, so a lookup checks about 3.9 runs (the same value as the tiered write curve). Tiered keeps up to T-1 runs per level: about 35 runs to check at T = 10.
Raising T shrinks the number of levels, which helps tiered writes but makes leveled writes worse: each level now rewrites more. The gap is 2x at T = 2 and 20x at T = 20.
A 13x larger dataset (R = 100,000) adds only about 1 level at T = 10, because levels grow geometrically. Costs scale with log of data size.

blocks.md: More runs would be fatal for point lookups without one more trick. Each SSTable stores a **Bloom filter**: a bit array that answers "definitely not in this file" or "maybe in this file". The false positive rate for $b$ bits per key and $k$ hash functions is about $(1 - e^{-k/b})^k$. RocksDB has no filter unless you configure one; the usual setting, 10 bits per key, gives roughly a 1% false positive rate.

blocks.title: Bloom filter false positive rate vs bits per key

scenes.caption: False positive rate in percent for a standard Bloom filter with the best number of hash functions (k = 1, 3, 7, 11). Each extra 4.8 or so bits per key buys roughly 10x fewer false positives.
Expected wasted file reads for a lookup of a missing key across 8 runs (4 L0 files + 4 levels): 3.15, 0.73, 0.066, 0.004. Without filters it would be 8 reads.

blocks.md: Bloom filters only help point lookups. A range scan must open every run that overlaps the range and merge them, so the RocksDB guide counts scan read amplification as (L0 files) + (non-empty levels). Tiered layouts with many runs pay most for scans.

Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

blocks.question: An ingest-heavy logging pipeline is limited by SSD write bandwidth and rarely reads old data. Which change most directly raises its sustainable write rate?
options: Switch from leveled to tiered (universal) compaction
Raise Bloom filter bits per key from 10 to 16
Lower the size ratio from 10 to 4 with leveled compaction
Use smaller memtables so flushes happen more often
blocks.explain: If compaction writes are the bottleneck, cutting write amplification from tens to a few multiplies the user write rate the disk can sustain. Bloom bits affect reads. In the model, lowering T for leveled only trims write cost slightly (38.9 to 25.9) while adding levels. Smaller memtables create more, smaller runs and more work.

blocks.question: A database uses 10 bits per key Bloom filters and has 8 sorted runs. A lookup for a key that exists only in the last run is issued. About how many file reads does it take, assuming filters and indexes are cached?
blocks.explain: The true hit costs 1 read. The 7 other runs each pass a false positive with about 0.82% probability: 7 x 0.0082 = 0.057 extra reads. Total about 1.06. 8 is the no-filter case; 0.07 is the expected cost for a missing key.

lessons.title: Choosing an engine: tradeoffs, write stalls and failure modes

blocks.md: Lesson by lesson we have three designs with different costs. A useful way to compare them is to put them on the same workload with the same assumptions: 1 billion keys, 100-byte rows, 8 KiB B+tree pages with the top levels cached, a leveled LSM with write amplification 33, and Bloom filters at 10 bits per key.

blocks.title: B+tree vs leveled LSM under this course's models

scenes.caption: Bytes written per random 100-byte update: a full 8 KiB page plus a 100-byte WAL record (8292), versus 33x write amplification plus the WAL record (3400). Both simplified.
Disk reads for a key that exists, with upper B+tree levels and all Bloom filters cached: 1 for the B+tree, about 1.06 for the LSM with 8 runs at 10 bits per key.
Disk reads for a missing key: the B+tree must read the leaf to learn the key is absent (1). LSM Bloom filters usually say no without any I/O: about 0.066 expected reads.
Sorted structures a range scan must merge: one B+tree versus 4 L0 files plus 4 levels = 8 runs. Scans are where LSM read amplification shows most.

blocks.md: Memory is part of the bill. The B+tree example needed about 33 MB to cache its inner levels. Bloom filters at 10 bits per key for 1 billion keys need $10^9 \times 10 / 8$ bytes = **1.25 GB**, plus SSTable index blocks. The RocksDB Bloom filter docs note that filters commonly use about 10% of system RAM. An LSM that cannot keep its filters cached loses most of its point-read advantage.

The biggest operational risk of an LSM-tree is **compaction debt**. Flushes are cheap and fast; compaction is the deferred bill. If compaction cannot keep up, L0 files pile up, every read checks more of them, and RocksDB eventually protects itself by slowing and then stopping writes.

blocks.title: When compaction falls behind: L0 files over time

scenes.caption: Model: each flush adds a 64 MB L0 file; draining one costs about 128 MB of compaction writes (L0 to L1 has write amp about 2). At 16 MB/s in and 24 MB/s of compaction, L0 grows 0.0625 files/s.
L0 hits RocksDB's default level0_slowdown_writes_trigger (20) at 256 s, and writes are throttled. At 36 files (level0_stop_writes_trigger) writes stop entirely, at 512 s.
Double the write rate to 32 MB/s: the slowdown arrives at 51 s and the stop at 102 s. Ingest bursts are absorbed only as long as compaction debt stays bounded.
Give compaction 40 MB/s and it keeps up: L0 stays at the 4-file trigger. Simplified: real engines also need bandwidth for deeper levels, and reads compete for the same disk.

blocks.md: Misconception: "LSM-trees have no write amplification because they only write sequentially." They write sequentially, but every byte is rewritten as it moves down levels: about 33x in RocksDB's leveled example. The win is in I/O pattern and batching, not in writing less, and on some workloads a B+tree writes fewer bytes.

How the choice usually falls out:

- **Read-mostly, range-heavy, latency-sensitive** (classic OLTP indexes): B+tree. One copy per key, one sorted structure to scan.
- **Write-heavy, many random inserts, high churn** (ingest, time series, logs, key-value caches backed by disk): LSM-tree, leveled if reads and space matter, tiered if write bandwidth is the limit.
- **Lots of lookups for absent keys** (dedup checks, "insert if not exists"): LSM-trees with Bloom filters can answer without I/O.

Sarkar et al.'s compaction design-space study breaks every compaction policy into four choices (trigger, data layout, granularity, data movement) and benchmarks 10 strategies: each choice moves cost between writes, reads, space and deletes.

No engine minimizes read, write and space amplification at once. B+trees pay on random writes. Leveled LSMs pay in rewrites. Tiered LSMs pay in reads and temporary space. Pick the cost your workload can afford, then tune T, Bloom bits and compaction bandwidth.

blocks.question: A team moves a write-heavy service to an LSM engine. After a week, p99 read latency climbs steadily while the write rate is constant, and disk utilization is at 100%. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bloom filters have too many bits per key
Compaction is not keeping up, so L0 files and sorted runs accumulate and each read checks more of them
The memtable is too small to hold recent writes
The WAL is being fsynced too rarely
blocks.explain: Rising read latency at a constant write rate with a saturated disk is the signature of compaction debt: more L0 files and runs per lookup, and compaction I/O competing with reads. More Bloom bits would help reads, not hurt them; WAL fsync policy affects durability and write latency.

blocks.question: Which workload most favors a B+tree over an LSM-tree?
options: Inserting billions of sensor readings per day with random keys
Checking whether each of millions of incoming ids already exists, where most do not
Frequent range scans over recent and old data with few updates
A cache layer that overwrites the same keys constantly
blocks.explain: Range scans with rare updates suit a single sorted structure: the B+tree walks sibling leaves, while an LSM must merge every overlapping run and Bloom filters cannot help. High-rate random inserts, absent-key checks and overwrite-heavy workloads all play to LSM strengths.

blocks.question: RocksDB universal compaction is configured on a 400 GB database on a 500 GB disk. What is the main risk?
options: Writes will stall because L0 has too many files
Bloom filters stop working above 100 GB
Read amplification drops to zero, wasting memory
A full compaction can temporarily need about 2x the data size in disk space
blocks.explain: In a major universal compaction the input runs and the output run coexist until it finishes, so space briefly approaches double the live data. The RocksDB docs warn to keep enough free space and, at large sizes, to shard into multiple instances.
